entries.85788c6300b17df73d2a5434c7e341862c437361: <div sID="gen17444" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="12" osisID="Jer.12" sID="Jer.12"/> <div eID="gen17444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17445" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17446" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. The prophet's humble complaint to God of the success that wicked people had in their wicked practices (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.1-Jer.12.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>) and his appeal to God concerning his own integrity (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.3">ver. 3</reference>), with a prayer that God would, for the sake of the public, bring the wickedness of the wicked to an end, <reference osisRef="Jer.12.3-Jer.12.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>. II. God's rebuke to the prophet for his uneasiness at his present troubles, bidding him prepare for greater, <reference osisRef="Jer.12.5-Jer.12.6">ver. 5, 6</reference>. III. A sad lamentation of the present deplorable state of the Israel of God, <reference osisRef="Jer.12.7-Jer.12.13">ver. 7-13</reference>. IV. An intimation of mercy to God's people, in a denunciation of wrath against their neighbours that helped forward their affliction, that they should be plucked out; but with a promise that if they would at last join themselves with the people of God they should come in sharers with them in their privileges, <reference osisRef="Jer.12.14-Jer.12.17">ver. 14-17</reference>.
entries.879a9d8f0030b4aba472eb19962ff77bc034c933: <div eID="gen17446" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17445" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Prophet's Appeal to God. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 606.)</title> <div sID="gen17447" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Righteous <hi type="italic">art</hi> thou, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , when I plead with thee: yet let me talk with thee of <hi type="italic">thy</hi> judgments: Wherefore doth the way of the wicked prosper? <hi type="italic">wherefore</hi> are all they happy that deal very treacherously? <hi type="super">2</hi> Thou hast planted them, yea, they have taken root: they grow, yea, they bring forth fruit: thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> near in their mouth, and far from their reins. <hi type="super">3</hi> But thou, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , knowest me: thou hast seen me, and tried mine heart toward thee: pull them out like sheep for the slaughter, and prepare them for the day of slaughter. <hi type="super">4</hi> How long shall the land mourn, and the herbs of every field wither, for the wickedness of them that dwell therein? the beasts are consumed, and the birds; because they said, He shall not see our last end. <hi type="super">5</hi> If thou hast run with the footmen, and they have wearied thee, then how canst thou contend with horses? and <hi type="italic">if</hi> in the land of peace, <hi type="italic">wherein</hi> thou trustedst, <hi type="italic">they wearied thee,</hi> then how wilt thou do in the swelling of Jordan? <hi type="super">6</hi> For even thy brethren, and the house of thy father, even they have dealt treacherously with thee; yea, they have called a multitude after thee: believe them not, though they speak fair words unto thee. <div eID="gen17447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17448" type="x-p"/> The prophet doubts not but it would be of use to others to know what had passed between God and his soul, what temptations he had been assaulted with and how he had got over them; and therefore he here tells us, <div eID="gen17448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17449" type="x-p"/> I. What liberty he humbly took, and was graciously allowed him, to reason with God concerning his judgments, <reference osisRef="Jer.12.1">v. 1</reference>. He is about to <hi type="italic">plead</hi> with God, not to quarrel with him, or find fault with his proceedings, but to enquire into the meaning of them, that he might more and more see reason to be satisfied in them, and might have wherewith to answer both his own and others' objections against them. The works of the Lord, and the reasons of them, are <hi type="italic">sought out</hi> even <hi type="italic">of those that have pleasure therein.</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.111.2">Ps. cxi. 2</reference>. We may not <hi type="italic">strive with our Maker,</hi> but we may reason with him. The prophet lays down a truth of unquestionable certainty, which he resolves to abide by in managing this argument: <hi type="italic">Righteous art thou, O Lord! when I plead with thee.</hi> Thus he arms himself against the temptation wherewith he was assaulted, to envy the prosperity of the wicked, before he entered into a parley with it. Note, When we are most in the dark concerning the meaning of God's dispensations we must still resolve to keep up right thoughts of God, and must be confident of this, that he never did, nor ever will do, the least wrong to any of his creatures; even when his <hi type="italic">judgments are</hi> unsearchable as <hi type="italic">a great deep,</hi> and altogether unaccountable, yet <hi type="italic">his righteousness</hi> is as conspicuous and immovable as <hi type="italic">the great mountains,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.36.6">Ps. xxxvi. 6</reference>. Though sometimes <hi type="italic">clouds and darkness are round about him,</hi> yet <hi type="italic">justice and judgment are</hi> always <hi type="italic">the habitation of his throne,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.97.2">Ps. xcvii. 2</reference>. When we find it hard to understand particular providences we must have recourse to general truths as our first principles, and abide by them; however dark the providence may be, <hi type="italic">the Lord is righteous;</hi> see <reference osisRef="Ps.73.1">Ps. lxxiii. 1</reference>. And we must acknowledge it to him, as the prophet here, even when we <hi type="italic">plead with him,</hi> as those that have no thoughts of contending but of learning, being fully assured that he will be <hi type="italic">justified when he speaks.</hi> Note, However we may see cause for our own information to plead with God, yet it becomes us to own that, whatever he says or does, he is in the right. <div eID="gen17449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17450" type="x-p"/> II. What it was in the dispensations of divine Providence that he stumbled at and that he thought would bear a debate. It was that which has been a temptation to many wise and good men, and such a one as they have with difficulty got over. They see the designs and projects of wicked people successful: <hi type="italic">The way of the wicked prospers;</hi> they compass their malicious designs and gain their point. They see their affairs and concerns in a good posture: <hi type="italic">They are happy,</hi> happy as the world can make them, though <hi type="italic">they deal</hi> treacherously, <hi type="italic">very treacherously,</hi> both with God and man. Hypocrites are chiefly meant (as appears, <reference osisRef="Jer.12.2">v. 2</reference>), who dissemble in their good professions, and depart from their good beginnings and good promises, and in both they deal treacherously, very treacherously. It has been said that men cannot expect to prosper who are unjust and dishonest in their dealings; but these deal treacherously, and yet <hi type="italic">they are happy.</hi> The prophet shows (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.2">v. 2</reference>) both their prosperity and their abuse of their prosperity. 1. God had been very indulgent to them and they were got beforehand in the world: "They are planted in a good land, a land flowing with milk and honey, and <hi type="italic">thou hast planted them!</hi> nay, thou didst cast out the heathen to plant them," <reference osisRef="Ps.44.2">Ps. xliv. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.80.8">lxxx. 8</reference>. Many a tree is planted that yet never grows nor comes to any thing; but <hi type="italic">they have taken root;</hi> their prosperity seems to be confirmed and settled. They take root in the earth, for there they fix themselves, and thence they draw the sap of all their satisfaction. Many trees however take root which yet never come on; but these <hi type="italic">grow, yea they bring forth fruit;</hi> their families are built up, they live high, and spend at a great rate; and all this was owing to the benignity of the divine Providence, which smiled upon them, <reference osisRef="Ps.73.7">Ps. lxxiii. 7</reference>. 2. Thus God had favoured them, though they had dealt treacherously with him: <hi type="italic">Thou art near in their mouth and far from their reins.</hi> This was no uncharitable censure, for he spoke by the Spirit of prophecy, without which it is not safe to charge men with hypocrisy whose appearances are plausible. Observe, (1.) Thought they cared not for thinking of God, nor had any sincere affection to him, yet they could easily persuade themselves to speak of him frequently and with an air of seriousness. Piety from the teeth outward is no difficult thing. Many speak the language of Israel that are not Israelites indeed. (2.) Though they had on all occasions the name of God ready in their mouth, and accustomed themselves to those forms of speech that savoured of piety, yet they could not persuade themselves to keep up the fear of God in their hearts. The form of godliness should engage us to keep up the power of it; but with them it did not do so. <div eID="gen17450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17451" type="x-p"/> III. What comfort he had in appealing to God concerning his own integrity (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">But thou, O Lord! knowest me.</hi> Probably the wicked men he complains of were forward to reproach and censure him (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.18">ch. xviii. 18</reference>), in reference to which this was his comfort, that God was a witness of his integrity. God knew he was not such a one as they were (who had God <hi type="italic">near in their mouths, but far from their reins</hi>), nor such a one as they took him to be, and represented him, a deceiver and a false prophet; those that thus abused him did not know him, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.8">1 Cor. ii. 8</reference>. "<hi type="italic">But thou, O Lord! knowest me,</hi> though they think me not worth their notice." 1. Observe what the matter is concerning which he appeals to God: Thou knowest <hi type="italic">my heart towards thee.</hi> Note, We are as our hearts are, and our hearts are good or bad according as they are, or are not, towards God; and this is that therefore concerning which we should examine ourselves, that we may approve ourselves to God. 2. The cognizance to which he appeals: <hi type="italic">"Thou knowest me</hi> better than I know myself, not by hearsay or report, for <hi type="italic">thou hast seen me,</hi> not with a transient glance, but thou hast <hi type="italic">tried my heart.</hi>" God's knowledge of us is as clear and exact and certain as if he had made the most strict scrutiny. Note, The God with whom we have to do perfectly knows how our hearts are towards him. He knows both the guile of the hypocrite and the sincerity of the upright. <div eID="gen17451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17452" type="x-p"/> IV. He prays that God would turn his hand against these wicked people, and not suffer them to prosper always, though they had prospered long: "Let some judgment come to <hi type="italic">pull them out</hi> of this fat pasture <hi type="italic">as sheep for the slaughter,</hi> that it may appear their long prosperity was but like the feeding of lambs in a large place, to <hi type="italic">prepare them for the day of slaughter,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Hos.4.16">Hos. iv. 16</reference>. God suffered them to prosper that by their pride and luxury they might fill up the measure of their iniquity and so be ripened for destruction; and therefore he thinks it a piece of necessary justice that they should fall into mischief themselves, because they had done so much mischief to others, that they should be pulled out of their land, because they had brought ruin upon the land, and the longer they continued in it the more hurt they did, as the plagues of their generation (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">How long shall the land mourn.</hi> (as it does under the judgments of God inflicted upon it) <hi type="italic">for the wickedness of those that dwell therein?</hi> Lord, shall those prosper themselves that ruin all about them?" 1. See here what the judgment was which the land was now groaning under: <hi type="italic">The herbs of every field wither</hi> (the grass is burnt up and all the products of the earth fail), and then it follows of course, the beasts are consumed, and the birds, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.5">1 Kings xviii. 5</reference>. This was the effect of a long drought, or want of rain, which happened, as it should seem, at the latter end of Josiah's reign and the beginning of Jehoiakim's; it is mentioned <reference osisRef="Jer.3.3">ch. iii. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.13">viii. 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.9.10">ix. 10,</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.9.12">12</reference>, and more fully afterwards, <reference osisRef="Jer.14.1-Jer.14.22">ch. xiv.</reference> If they would have been brought to repentance by this less judgment, the greater would have been prevented. Now why was it that this <hi type="italic">fruitful land</hi> was <hi type="italic">turned into barrenness,</hi> but <hi type="italic">for the wickedness of those that dwelt therein?</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.17.34">Ps. xvii. 34</reference>. Therefore the prophet prays that these wicked people might <hi type="italic">die for their own sin,</hi> and that the whole nation might not suffer for it. 2. See here what was the language of their wickedness: <hi type="italic">They said, He shall not see our last end,</hi> either, (1.) God himself shall not. Atheism is the root of hypocrisy. God is <hi type="italic">far from their reins,</hi> though <hi type="italic">near in their mouth,</hi> because they say, <hi type="italic">How doth God know?</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.73.11">Ps. lxxiii. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.22.13">Job xxii. 13</reference>. He knows not what way we take nor what it will end in. Or, (2.) Jeremiah <hi type="italic">shall not see our last end;</hi> whatever he pretends, when he asks us what shall be in the end hereof he cannot himself foresee it. They look upon him as a false prophet. Or, "whatever it is, he shall not live to see it, for we will be the death of him," <reference osisRef="Jer.11.21">ch. xi. 21</reference>. Note, [1.] Men's setting their latter end at a great distance, or looking upon it as uncertain, is at the bottom of all their wickedness, <reference osisRef="Lam.1.9">Lam. i. 9</reference>. [2.] The whole creation groans under the burden of the sin of man, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.22">Rom. viii. 22</reference>. It is for this that <hi type="italic">the earth mourns</hi> (so it may be read); <hi type="italic">cursed is the ground for thy sake.</hi> <div eID="gen17452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17453" type="x-p"/> V. He acquaints us with the answer God gave to those complaints of his, <reference osisRef="Jer.12.5-Jer.12.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. We often find the prophets admonished, whose business it was to admonish others, as <reference osisRef="Isa.8.11">Isa. viii. 11</reference>. Ministers have lessons to learn as well as lessons to teach, and must themselves hear God's voice and preach to themselves. Jeremiah complained much of the wickedness of the men of Anathoth, and that, notwithstanding that, they prospered. Now, this seems to be an answer to that complaint. 1. It is allowed that he had cause to complain (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thy brethren,</hi> the priests of Anathoth, who are of <hi type="italic">the house of thy father,</hi> who ought to have protected thee and pretended to do so, <hi type="italic">even they have dealt treacherously with thee,</hi> have been false to thee, and, under colour of friendship, have designedly done thee all the mischief they could; they <hi type="italic">have called a multitude after thee,</hi> raised the mob upon thee, to whom they have endeavoured, by all arts possible, to render thee despicable or odious, while at the same time they pretended that they had no design to persecute thee nor to deprive thee of thy liberty. They are indeed such as thou canst <hi type="italic">not believe, though they speak fair words to thee.</hi> They seem to be thy friends, but are really thy enemies." Note, God's faithful servants must not think it at all strange if their foes be <hi type="italic">those of their own house</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.36">Matt. x. 36</reference>), and if those they expect kindness from prove such as they can put no confidence in, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.5">Mic. vii. 5</reference>. 2. Yet he is told that he carried the matter too far. (1.) He laid the unkindness of his countrymen too much to heart. <hi type="italic">They wearied</hi> him, because it was <hi type="italic">in a land of peace wherein he trusted,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.12.5">v. 5</reference>. It was very grievous to him to be thus hated and abused by his own kindred. He was disturbed in his mind by it; his spirit was sunk and overwhelmed with it, so that he was in great agitation and distress about it. Nay, he was discouraged in his work by it, began to be weary of prophesying, and to think of giving it up. (2.) He did not consider that this was but the beginning of his sorrow, and that he had sorer trials yet before him; and, whereas he should endeavour by a patient bearing of this trouble to prepare himself for greater, by his uneasiness under this he did but unfit himself for what further lay before him: <hi type="italic">If thou hast run with the footmen and they have wearied thee,</hi> and run thee quite out of breath,<hi type="italic">then how wilt thou contend with horses?</hi> If the injuries done him by the men of Anathoth made such an impression upon him, what would he do when the princes and chief priests at Jerusalem should set upon him with their power, as they did afterwards? <reference osisRef="Jer.20.2">ch. xx. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.32.2">xxxii. 2</reference>. If he was so soon tired <hi type="italic">in a land of peace,</hi> where there was little noise or peril, <hi type="italic">what would he do in the swellings of Jordan,</hi> when that overflows all its banks and frightens even lions out of their thickets? <reference osisRef="Jer.49.19">ch. xlix. 19</reference>. Note, [1.] While we are in this world we must expect troubles, and difficulties. Our life is a race, a warfare; we are in danger of being run down. [2.] God's usual method being to begin with smaller trials, it is our wisdom to expect greater than any we have yet met with. We may be called out to <hi type="italic">contend with horsemen,</hi> and the sons of Anak may perhaps be reserved for the last encounter. [3.] It highly concerns us to prepare for such trials and to consider what we should do in them. How shall we preserve our integrity and peace when we come to <hi type="italic">the swellings of Jordan?</hi> [4.] In order to our preparation for further and greater trials, we are concerned to approve ourselves well in present smaller trials, to keep up our spirits, keep hold of the promise, keep in our way, with our eye upon the prize, so run that we may obtain it. Some good interpreters understand this as spoken to the people, who were very secure and fearless of the threatened judgments. If they have been so humbled and impoverished by smaller calamities, so wasted by the Assyrians,—if the Ammonites and Moabites, who were their brethren, and with whom they were in league, proved false to them (as undoubtedly they would),—then how would they be able to deal with such a powerful adversary as the Chaldeans would be? How would they bear up their head against that invasion which should come like <hi type="italic">the swelling of Jordan?</hi>
entries.a964c4c4815f726a4d2c93b3c073753daaefe800: <div eID="gen17453" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The State of Judah and Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 606.)</title> <div sID="gen17454" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> I have forsaken mine house, I have left mine heritage; I have given the dearly beloved of my soul into the hand of her enemies. <hi type="super">8</hi> Mine heritage is unto me as a lion in the forest; it crieth out against me: therefore have I hated it. <hi type="super">9</hi> Mine heritage <hi type="italic">is</hi> unto me <hi type="italic">as</hi> a speckled bird, the birds round about <hi type="italic">are</hi> against her; come ye, assemble all the beasts of the field, come to devour. <hi type="super">10</hi> Many pastors have destroyed my vineyard, they have trodden my portion under foot, they have made my pleasant portion a desolate wilderness. <hi type="super">11</hi> They have made it desolate, <hi type="italic">and being</hi> desolate it mourneth unto me; the whole land is made desolate, because no man layeth <hi type="italic">it</hi> to heart. <hi type="super">12</hi> The spoilers are come upon all high places through the wilderness: for the sword of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall devour from the <hi type="italic">one</hi> end of the land even to the <hi type="italic">other</hi> end of the land: no flesh shall have peace. <hi type="super">13</hi> They have sown wheat, but shall reap thorns: they have put themselves to pain, <hi type="italic">but</hi> shall not profit: and they shall be ashamed of your revenues because of the fierce anger of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen17454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17455" type="x-p"/> The people of the Jews are here marked for ruin. <div eID="gen17455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17456" type="x-p"/> I. God is here brought in falling out with them and leaving them desolate; and they could never have been undone if they had not provoked God to desert them. It is a terrible word that God here says (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">I have forsaken my house</hi>—the temple, which had been his palace; they had polluted it, and so forced him out of it: <hi type="italic">I have left my heritage,</hi> and will look after it no more. His people that he has taken such delight in, and care of, are now thrown out of his protection. They had been <hi type="italic">the dearly beloved of his soul,</hi> precious in his sight and honorable above any people, which is mentioned to aggravate their sin in returning him hatred for his love and their misery in throwing themselves out of the favour of one that had such a kindness for them, and to justify God in his dealings with them. He sought not occasion against them, but, if they would have conducted themselves with any tolerable propriety, he would have made the best of them, for they were <hi type="italic">the beloved of his soul;</hi> but they had conducted themselves so that they had provoked him to <hi type="italic">give them into the hand of their enemies,</hi> to leave them unguarded, an easy prey to those that bore them ill-will. But what was the quarrel God had with a people that had been so long dear to him? Why, truly, they had degenerated. 1. They had become like <hi type="italic">beasts of prey,</hi> which nobody loves, but every body avoids and gets as far off from as he can (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">My heritage is unto me as a lion in the forest.</hi> Their sins cry to heaven for vengeance as loud as a lion roars. Nay, they <hi type="italic">cry out against God</hi> in the threatenings and slaughter which they breathe against his prophets that speak to them in his name; and what is said and done against them God takes as said and done against himself. They blaspheme his name, oppose his authority, and bid defiance to his justice, and so <hi type="italic">cry out against him as a lion in the forest.</hi> Those that were the <hi type="italic">sheep of God's pasture</hi> had become barbarous and ravenous, and as ungovernable as lions in the forest; <hi type="italic">therefore he hated them;</hi> for what delight could the God of love take in a people that had now become as roaring lions and raging beasts, fit to be taken and shot at, as a vexation and torment to all about them? 2. They had become like <hi type="italic">birds of prey,</hi> and therefore also unworthy a place in God's house, where neither beasts nor birds of prey were admitted to be offered in sacrifice (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">My heritage is unto me as a bird with talons</hi> (so some read it, and so the margin); they are continually pulling and pecking at one another; they have by their unnatural contentions made their country a cock-pit. Or <hi type="italic">as a speckled bird,</hi> dyed, or sprinkled, or bedewed with the blood of her prey. The shedding of innocent blood was Jerusalem's measure-filling sin, and hastened their ruin, not only as it provoked their neighbours likewise; for those that have <hi type="italic">their hand against every man</hi> shall have <hi type="italic">every man's hand against them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.16.12">Gen. xvi. 12</reference>), and so it follows here: <hi type="italic">The birds round about are against her.</hi> Some make her a <hi type="italic">speckled, pied,</hi> or <hi type="italic">motley bird,</hi> upon the account of their mixing the superstitious customs and usages of the heathen with divine institutions in the worship of God; they were fond of a party-coloured religion, and thought it made them fine, when really it made them odious. God's turtle-dove is no speckled bird. <div eID="gen17456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17457" type="x-p"/> II. The enemies are here brought in falling upon them and laying them desolate. And some think it is upon this account that they are compared to a speckled bird, because fowls usually make a noise about a bird of an odd unusual colour. God's people are, among the children of this world, as <hi type="italic">men wondered at,</hi> as a <hi type="italic">speckled bird;</hi> but this people had by their own folly made themselves so; and the beasts and birds are called and commissioned to prey upon them. Let <hi type="italic">all the birds round</hi> be <hi type="italic">against her,</hi> for God has forsaken her, and with them let <hi type="italic">all the beasts of the field come to devour.</hi> Those that have made a prey of others shall themselves be preyed upon. It did not lessen the sin of the nations, but very much increased the misery of Judah and Jerusalem, that the desolation brought upon them was by order from heaven. The birds and beasts are perhaps called to feast upon the bodies of the slain, as in St. John's vision, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.17-Rev.19.18">Rev. xix. 17, 18</reference>. The utter desolation of the land by the Chaldean army is here spoken of as a thing done, so sure, so near, was it. God speaks of it as a thing which he had appointed to be done, and yet which he had no pleasure in, any more than in the death of other sinners. <div eID="gen17457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17458" type="x-p"/> 1. See with what a tender affection he speaks of this land, notwithstanding the sinfulness of it, in remembrance of his covenant, and the tribute of honour and glory he had formerly had from it: It is <hi type="italic">my vineyard, my portion, my pleasant portion,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.12.10">v. 10</reference>. Note, God has a kindness and concern for his church, though there be much amiss in it; and his correcting it will every way consist with his complacency in it. <div eID="gen17458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17459" type="x-p"/> 2. See with what a tender compassion he speaks of the desolations of this land: <hi type="italic">Many pastors</hi> (the Chaldean generals that made themselves masters of the country and ate it up with their armies as easily as the Arabian shepherds with their flocks eat up the fruits of a piece of ground that lies common) <hi type="italic">have destroyed my vineyard,</hi> without any consideration had either of the value of it or of my interest in it; they have with the greatest insolence and indignation <hi type="italic">trodden it under foot,</hi> and that which was a pleasant land they have made <hi type="italic">a desolate wilderness.</hi> The destruction was universal: <hi type="italic">The whole land is made desolate,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.12.11">v. 11</reference>. It is made so by the sword of war: <hi type="italic">The spoilers,</hi> the Chaldean soldiers, <hi type="italic">have come through the plain upon all high places;</hi> they have made themselves masters of all the natural fastnesses and artificial fortresses, <reference osisRef="Jer.12.12">v. 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">The sword devours from one end of the land to the other;</hi> all places lie exposed, and the numerous army of the invaders disperse themselves into every corner of that fruitful country, so that <hi type="italic">no flesh shall have peace,</hi> none shall be exempt from the calamity nor be able to enjoy any tranquillity. When all flesh have corrupted their way, no flesh shall have peace; those only have peace that walk after the Spirit. <div eID="gen17459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17460" type="x-p"/> 3. See whence all this misery comes. (1.) It comes from the displeasure of God. It is <hi type="italic">the sword of the Lord</hi> that <hi type="italic">devours,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.12.12">v. 12</reference>. While God's people keep close to him the sword of their protectors and deliverers is the sword of the Lord, witness that of Gideon; but when they have forsaken him, so that he has become their enemy and fights against them, then the sword of their invaders and destroyers becomes the <hi type="italic">sword of the Lord;</hi> witness this of the Chaldeans. It is <hi type="italic">because of the fierce anger of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.13">v. 13</reference>); it was this that kindled this fire among them and made their enemies so furious. And <hi type="italic">who may stand before him when he is angry?</hi> (2.) It is their sin that has made God their enemy, particularly their incorrigibleness under former rebukes (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.11">v. 11</reference>): The land <hi type="italic">mourns unto me;</hi> the country that lies desolate does, as it were, pour out its complaint before God and humble itself under his hand; but the inhabitants are so senseless and stupid that <hi type="italic">none of them lays it to heart;</hi> they do not mourn to God, but are unaffected with his displeasure, while the very ground they go upon shames them. Note, When God's hand is lifted up, and men will not see, it shall be laid on, and they shall be made to feel, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.11">Isa. xxvi. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen17460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17461" type="x-p"/> 4. See how unable they should be to guard against it (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.13">v. 13</reference>): "<hi type="italic">They have sown wheat,</hi> that is, they have taken a great deal of pains for their own security and promised themselves great matters from their endeavors, but it is all in vain; <hi type="italic">they shall reap thorns,</hi> that is, that which shall prove very grievous and vexatious to them. Instead of helping themselves, they shall but make themselves more uneasy. <hi type="italic">They have put themselves to pain,</hi> both with their labour and with their expectations, <hi type="italic">but it shall not profit;</hi> they shall not prevail to extricate themselves out of the difficulties into which they have plunged themselves. <hi type="italic">They shall be ashamed of your revenues,</hi> ashamed that they have depended so much upon their preparations for war and particularly upon their ability to bear the charges of it." Money constitutes the sinews of war; they thought they had enough of that, but shall be ashamed of it; for their silver and gold shall not profit them in the day of the Lord's anger.
entries.e76674dc00b31e79cfa90832c1d45207b74dc9e0: <div eID="gen17461" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Predictions of Mercy. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 606.)</title> <div sID="gen17462" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> against all mine evil neighbours, that touch the inheritance which I have caused my people Israel to inherit; Behold, I will pluck them out of their land, and pluck out the house of Judah from among them. <hi type="super">15</hi> And it shall come to pass, after that I have plucked them out I will return, and have compassion on them, and will bring them again, every man to his heritage, and every man to his land. <hi type="super">16</hi> And it shall come to pass, if they will diligently learn the ways of my people, to swear by my name, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> liveth; as they taught my people to swear by Baal; then shall they be built in the midst of my people. <hi type="super">17</hi> But if they will not obey, I will utterly pluck up and destroy that nation, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen17462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17463" type="x-p"/> The prophets sometimes, in God's name, delivered messages both of judgment and mercy to the nations that bordered on the land of Israel: but here is a message to all those in general who had in their turns been one way or other injurious to God's people, had either oppressed them or triumphed in their being oppressed. Observe, <div eID="gen17463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17464" type="x-p"/> I. What the quarrel was that God had with them. They were <hi type="italic">his evil neighbours</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.14">v. 14</reference>), evil neighbours to his church, and what they did against it he took as done against himself, and therefore called them <hi type="italic">his evil neighbours,</hi> that should have been neighbourly to Israel, but were quite otherwise. Note, It is often the lot of good people to live among bad neighbours, that are unkind and provoking to them; and it is bad indeed when they are all so. These evil neighbours were the Moabites, Ammonites, Syrians, Edomites, Egyptians, that had been evil neighbours to Israel in helping to debauch them and draw them from God (therefore God calls them his evil neighbours), and now they helped to make them desolate, and joined with the Chaldeans against them. It is just with God to make those the instruments of trouble to us whom we have made instruments of sin. That which God lays to their charge is: They have <hi type="italic">meddled with the inheritance which I have caused my people Israel to inherit;</hi> they unjustly seized that which was none of their own: nay, they sacrilegiously turned that to their own use which was given to God's peculiar people. He that said, <hi type="italic">Touch not my anointed,</hi> said also, "<hi type="italic">Touch not their inheritance;</hi> it is at your peril if you do." Not only the persons but the estates of God's people are under his protection. <div eID="gen17464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17465" type="x-p"/> II. What course he would take with them. 1. He would break the power they had got over his people, and force them to make restitution: <hi type="italic">I will pluck out the house of Judah from among them.</hi> This would be a great favour to God's people, who had either been taken captive by them, or, when they fled to them for shelter, had been detained and made prisoners; but it would be a great mortification to their enemies, who would be like a lion disappointed of his prey. The house of Judah either cannot or will not make any bold struggles towards their own liberty; but God will with a gracious violence pluck them out, will by his Spirit compel them to come out and by his power compel their task-masters to let them go, as he plucked Israel out of Egypt. 2. He would bring upon them the same calamities that they had been instrumental to bring upon his people: <hi type="italic">I will pluck them out of their land.</hi> Judgment began at the house of God, but it did not end there. Nebuchadnezzar, when he had wasted the land of Israel, turned his hand against their evil neighbours and was a scourge to them. <div eID="gen17465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17466" type="x-p"/> III. What mercy God had in store for such of them as would join themselves to him and become his people, <reference osisRef="Jer.12.15-Jer.12.16">v. 15, 16</reference>. They had drawn in God's backsliding people to join with them in the service of idols. If now they would be drawn by a returning people to join with them in the service of the true and living God, they should not only have their enmity to the people of God forgiven them, but the distance which they had been kept at before should be removed, and they should be received to stand upon the same level with the Israel of God. This had its accomplishment in part when, after the return out of captivity, many of the people of the lands that had been evil neighbours to Israel became Jews; and it was to have its accomplishment in the conversion of the Gentiles to the faith of Christ. Let not Israel, though injured by them, be implacable towards them, for God is not: <hi type="italic">After that I have plucked them out,</hi> in justice for their sins and in jealousy for the honour of Israel, <hi type="italic">I will return,</hi> will change my way, <hi type="italic">and have compassion on them.</hi> Though, being heathen, they can lay no claim to the mercies of the covenant, yet they shall have benefit by the compassions of the Creator, who will notwithstanding look upon them as the work of his hands. Note, God's controversies with his creatures, though they cannot be disputed, may be accommodated. Those who (as these) have been not only strangers, but <hi type="italic">enemies in their minds by wicked works,</hi> may be <hi type="italic">reconciled,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.1.21">Col. i. 21</reference>. Observe here, <div eID="gen17466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17467" type="x-p"/> 1. What were the terms on which God would show favour to them. It is always provided <hi type="italic">that they will diligently learn the ways of my people,</hi> that is, in general, the ways that they walk in when they conduct themselves as <hi type="italic">my people</hi> (not the crooked ways into which they have turned aside), the ways which my people are directed to take. Note, (1.) There are good ways that are peculiarly <hi type="italic">the ways of God's people,</hi> which however they may differ in the choice of their paths, they are all agreed to walk in. The ways of holiness and heavenly-mindedness, of love and peaceableness, the ways of prayer and sabbath-sanctification, and diligent attendance on instituted ordinances—these, and the like, are <hi type="italic">the ways of God's people.</hi> (2.) Those that would have their lot with God's people, and their last end like theirs, must learn their ways and walk in them, must observe the rule they walk by and conform to that rule they walk by and conform to that rule and go forth by those footsteps. By an intimate conversation with God's people they must learn to do as they do. (3.) It is impossible to learn the ways of God's people as they should be learnt, without a great deal of care and pains. We must diligently observe these ways and diligently obliges ourselves to walk in them, must look diligently (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.15">Heb. xii. 15</reference>), and work diligently, <reference osisRef="Luke.13.24">Luke xiii. 24</reference>. In particular, they must learn to give honour to God's name by making all their solemn appeals to him. They must learn to say, <hi type="italic">The Lord liveth</hi> (to own him, to adore him, and to abide by his judgment), <hi type="italic">as they taught my people to swear by Baal.</hi> It was bad enough that they did themselves swear by Baal, worse that they taught God's own people, who had been better taught; and yet, if they will at length reform, they shall be accepted. Observe, [1.] We must not despair of the conversion of the worst; no, not of those who have been instrumental to pervert and debauch others; even they may be brought to repentance, and, if they be, shall find mercy. [2.] Those whom we have been industrious to draw to that which is evil, when God opens their eyes and ours, we should be as industrious to follow in that which is good. It will be a holy revenge upon ourselves to become pupils to those in the way of duty to whom we have been tutors in the was of sin. [3.] The conversion of the deceived may prove a happy occasion of the conversion even of the deceivers. Thus those who fall together into the ditch are sometimes plucked together out of it. <div eID="gen17467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17468" type="x-p"/> 2. What should be the tokens and fruits of this favour when they return to God and God to them. (1.) They shall be restored to and re-established in their own land (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will bring them again every man to his heritage.</hi> The same hand that plucked them up shall plant them again. (2.) They shall become entitled to the spiritual privileges of God's Israel: "If they will be towardly, and <hi type="italic">learn the ways of my people,</hi> will conform to the rules and confine themselves to the restraints of my family, <hi type="italic">then shall they be built in the midst of my people.</hi> They shall not only be brought among them, to have a name and a place in the house of the Lord, where there was a court for the Gentiles, but they shall be built among them; they shall unite with them; the former enmities shall be slain; they shall be both edified and settled among them." See <reference osisRef="Isa.56.5-Isa.56.7">Isa. lvi. 5-7</reference>. Note, Those that diligently learn the ways of God's people shall enjoy the privileges and comforts of his people. <div eID="gen17468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17469" type="x-p"/> IV. What should become of those that were still wedded to their own evil ways, yea, though many of those about them turned to the Lord (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">If there will not obey,</hi> if any of them continue to stand it out, <hi type="italic">I will utterly pluck up and destroy that nation,</hi> that family, that particular person, <hi type="italic">saith the Lord.</hi> Those that will not be ruled by the grace of God shall be ruined by the justice of God. And, if disobedient nations shall be destroyed, much more disobedient churches from whom better things are expected.  <chapter eID="Jer.12"/> <div eID="gen17469" type="x-p"/>

entries.30a41a562fbafc17803acf9fa82d46fb4d6b7f79: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9865"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 12</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.12.1-Jer.12.17">Jr 12:1-17</reference>. Continuation of the Subject at the Close of the Eleventh Chapter.</title> <div sID="gen17494" type="x-p"/> He ventures to expostulate with Jehovah as to the prosperity of the wicked, who had plotted against his life (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.1-Jer.12.4">Jr 12:1-4</reference>); in reply he is told that he will have worse to endure, and that from his own relatives (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.5">Jr 12:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.12.6">6</reference>). The heaviest judgments, however, would be inflicted on the faithless people (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.7-Jer.12.13">Jr 12:7-13</reference>); and then on the nations co-operating with the Chaldeans against Judah, with, however, a promise of mercy on repentance (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.14-Jer.12.17">Jr 12:14-17</reference>).<div eID="gen17494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17495" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9865"/>1. (<reference osisRef="Ps.51.4">Psa 51:4</reference>).<div eID="gen17495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17496" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let me talk, &c.--</hi>only let me reason the case with Thee: inquire of Thee the causes why such wicked men as these plotters against my life prosper (compare <reference osisRef="Job.12.6">Job 12:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.21.7">21:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.37.1">Psa 37:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.35">35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.73.3">73:3</reference>; Mal 3:15). It is right, when hard thoughts of God's providence suggest themselves, to fortify our minds by justifying God beforehand (as did Jeremiah), even before we hear the reasons of His dealings. <div eID="gen17496" type="x-p"/>
entries.61f5beb9963835879de55a80481ba0c5c14c40ca: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9866"/><div sID="gen17497" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9866"/><hi type="bold">2. grow--</hi>literally, "go on," "progress." Thou givest them sure dwellings and increasing prosperity.<div eID="gen17497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17498" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">near in ... mouth ... far from ... reins--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.29.13">Is 29:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.15.8">Mt 15:8</reference>). Hypocrites. <div eID="gen17498" type="x-p"/>
entries.e9758f0989a300fc5729e171bef60c7d4e9b5796: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9867"/><div sID="gen17499" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9867"/><hi type="bold">3. knowest me--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.139.1">Psa 139:1</reference>).<div eID="gen17499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17500" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tried ... heart--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.11.20">Jr 11:20</reference>).<div eID="gen17500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17501" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">toward thee--</hi>rather, "with Thee," that is, entirely devoted to Thee; contrasted with the hypocrites (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.2">Jr 12:2</reference>), "near in ... mouth, and far from ... reins." This being so, how is it that I fare so ill, they so well?<div eID="gen17501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17502" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pull ... out--</hi>containing the metaphor, from a "rooted tree" (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.2">Jr 12:2</reference>).<div eID="gen17502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17503" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prepare--</hi>literally, "separate," or "set apart as devoted."<div eID="gen17503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17504" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">day of slaughter--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jas.5.5">Jas 5:5</reference>). <div eID="gen17504" type="x-p"/>
entries.e7881f069bd7ca585f60d8633a69569a2bef501f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9868"/><div sID="gen17505" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9868"/><hi type="bold">4. land mourn--</hi>personification (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.2">Jr 14:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.10">23:10</reference>).<div eID="gen17505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17506" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for the wickedness--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.107.34">Psa 107:34</reference>).<div eID="gen17506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17507" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">beasts--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hos.4.3">Ho 4:3</reference>).<div eID="gen17507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17508" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">He shall not see our last end--</hi>Jehovah knows not what is about to happen to us (<reference osisRef="Jer.5.12">Jr 5:12</reference>) [Rosenmuller]. So the Septuagint. (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.11">Psa 10:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.12">Eze 8:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.9">9:9</reference>). Rather, "The prophet (Jeremiah, to whom the whole context refers) shall not see our last end." We need not trouble ourselves about his boding predictions. We shall not be destroyed as he says (<reference osisRef="Jer.5.12">Jr 5:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.5.13">13</reference>). <div eID="gen17508" type="x-p"/>
entries.badbee42a20baf543e2c9d5d5b1d14d6def5db8d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9869"/><div sID="gen17509" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9869"/>5. Jehovah's reply to Jeremiah's complaint.<div eID="gen17509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17510" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">horses--</hi>that is, horsemen: the argument a fortiori. A proverbial phrase. The injuries done thee by the men of Anathoth ("the footmen") are small compared with those which the men of Jerusalem ("the horsemen") are about to inflict on thee. If the former weary thee out, how wilt thou contend with the king, the court, and the priests at Jerusalem?<div eID="gen17510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17511" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wherein thou trustedst, they wearied thee--</hi>English Version thus fills up the sentence with the italicized words, to answer to the parallel clause in the first sentence of the verse. The parallelism is, however, sufficiently retained with a less ellipsis: "If (it is only) in a land of peace thou art confident" [Maurer].<div eID="gen17511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17512" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">swelling of Jordan--</hi>In harvest-time and earlier (April and May) it overflows its banks (<reference osisRef="Josh.3.15">Jos 3:15</reference>), and fills the valley called the Ghor. Or, "the pride of Jordan," namely, its wooded banks abounding in lions and other wild beasts (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.19">Jr 49:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.44">50:44</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.11.3">Zec 11:3</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.2">2Ki 6:2</reference>). Maundrell says that between the Sea of Tiberias and Lake Merom the banks are so wooded that the traveller cannot see the river at all without first passing through the woods. If in the champaign country (alone) thou art secure, how wilt thou do when thou fallest into the wooded haunts of wild beasts? <div eID="gen17512" type="x-p"/>
entries.ee6afe9dec58e3ce8463bd8b75fa1c12ed570915: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9870"/><div sID="gen17513" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9870"/><hi type="bold">6. even thy brethren--</hi>as in Christ's case (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.8">Psa 69:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.1.11">Joh 1:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.5">7:5</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Jer.9.4">Jr 9:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.11.19">11:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.21">21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.10.36">Mt 10:36</reference>). Godly faithfulness is sure to provoke the ungodly, even of one's own family.<div eID="gen17513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17514" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">called a multitude after thee--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.31.4">Is 31:4</reference>). Jerome translates, "cry after thee with a loud (literally, 'full') voice."<div eID="gen17514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17515" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">believe ... not ... though ... speak fair--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.26.25">Pr 26:25</reference>). <div eID="gen17515" type="x-p"/>
entries.610680adcd0426236533d6870d341eac7cf46b21: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9871"/><div sID="gen17516" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9871"/><hi type="bold">7. I have forsaken--</hi>Jehovah will forsake His temple and the people peculiarly His. The mention of God's close tie to them, as heretofore His, aggravates their ingratitude, and shows that their past spiritual privileges will not prevent God from punishing them.<div eID="gen17516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17517" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">beloved of my soul--</hi>image from a wife (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.15">Jr 11:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.54.5">Is 54:5</reference>). <div eID="gen17517" type="x-p"/>
entries.f05125b1903d8d778c350387b3fd7a41e1feb6d6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9872"/><div sID="gen17518" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9872"/><hi type="bold">8. is unto me--</hi>is become unto Me: behaves towards Me as a lion which roars against a man, so that he withdraws from the place where he hears it: so I withdrew from My people, once beloved, but now an object of abhorrence because of their rebellious cries against Me. <div eID="gen17518" type="x-p"/>
entries.d369146030223a67df46093c6f2495807757c701: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9873"/><div sID="gen17519" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9873"/><hi type="bold">9. speckled bird--</hi>Many translate, "a ravenous beast, the hyena"; the corresponding Arabic word means hyena; so the Septuagint. But the Hebrew always elsewhere means "a bird of prey." The Hebrew for "speckled" is from a root "to color"; answering to the Jewish blending together with paganism the altogether diverse Mosaic ritual. The neighboring nations, birds of prey like herself (for she had sinfully assimilated herself to them), were ready to pounce upon her.<div eID="gen17519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17520" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">assemble ... beasts of ... field--</hi>The Chaldeans are told to gather the surrounding heathen peoples as allies against Judah (<reference osisRef="Isa.56.9">Is 56:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.5">Eze 34:5</reference>). <div eID="gen17520" type="x-p"/>
entries.e8dfef6579274a3e5d47b8a4f01f1df727dec98a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9874"/><div sID="gen17521" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9874"/><hi type="bold">10. pastors--</hi>the Babylonian leaders (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.12.12">Jr 12:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.3">Jr 6:3</reference>).<div eID="gen17521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17522" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my vineyard--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.5.1">Is 5:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.5">5</reference>).<div eID="gen17522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17523" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">trodden my portion--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.63.18">Is 63:18</reference>). <div eID="gen17523" type="x-p"/>
entries.b77dc3c1876240b24653a48184e1982562d444f1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9875"/><div sID="gen17524" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9875"/><hi type="bold">11. mourneth unto me--</hi>that is, before Me. Eichorn translates, "by reason of Me," because I have given it to desolation (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.7">Jr 12:7</reference>).<div eID="gen17524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17525" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because no man layeth it to heart--</hi>because none by repentance and prayer seek to deprecate God's wrath. Or, "yet none lays it to heart"; as in <reference osisRef="Jer.5.3">Jr 5:3</reference> [Calvin]. <div eID="gen17525" type="x-p"/>
entries.34597880d6ccc7842b2fab4968a89a7c1b68c6af: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9876"/><div sID="gen17526" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9876"/><hi type="bold">12. high places--</hi>Before, He had threatened the plains; now, the hills.<div eID="gen17526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17527" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wilderness--</hi>not an uninhabited desert, but high lands of pasturage, lying between Judea and Chaldea (<reference osisRef="Jer.4.11">Jr 4:11</reference>). <div eID="gen17527" type="x-p"/>
entries.0c45a1e2819e4f15cca01dad2007469d368750cc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9877"/><div sID="gen17528" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9877"/>13. Description in detail of the devastation of the land (<reference osisRef="Mic.6.15">Mi 6:15</reference>).<div eID="gen17528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17529" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they shall be ashamed of your--</hi>The change of persons, in passing from indirect to direct address, is frequent in the prophets. Equivalent to, "Ye shall be put to the shame of disappointment at the smallness of your produce." <div eID="gen17529" type="x-p"/>
entries.c611d82eb29fb9ff20d6b2e4e1826647edd4f1fc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9878"/><div sID="gen17530" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9878"/>14-17. Prophecy as to the surrounding nations, the Syrians, Ammonites, &c., who helped forward Judah's calamity: they shall share her fall; and, on their conversion, they shall share with her in the future restoration. This is a brief anticipation of the predictions in the forty-seventh, forty-eighth, and forty-ninth chapters.<div eID="gen17530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17531" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">touch--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Zech.2.8">Zec 2:8</reference>).<div eID="gen17531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17532" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pluck them out ... pluck out ... Judah--</hi>(Compare end of <reference osisRef="Jer.12.16">Jr 12:16</reference>). During the thirteen years that the Babylonians besieged Tyre, Nebuchadnezzar, after subduing Coelo-Syria, brought Ammon, Moab, &c., and finally Egypt, into subjection [Josephus, Antiquities, 10:9.7]. On the restoration of these nations, they were to exchange places with the Jews. The latter were now in the midst of them, but on their restoration they were to be "in the midst of the Jews," that is, as proselytes to the true God (compare <reference osisRef="Mic.5.7">Mi 5:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.16">Zec 14:16</reference>). "Pluck them," namely, the Gentile nations: in a bad sense. "Pluck Judah": in a good sense; used to express the force which was needed to snatch Judah from the tyranny of those nations by whom they had been made captives, or to whom they had fled; otherwise they never would have let Judah go. Previously he had been forbidden to pray for the mass of the Jewish people. But here he speaks consolation to the elect remnant among them. Whatever the Jews might be, God keeps His covenant. <div eID="gen17532" type="x-p"/>

entries.8875ea93268691ad73ca15d59e2e12b432f44bb9: <div eID="gen29560" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen29561" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29562" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29562" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29561" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29563" type="x-p"/> This chapter is connected with the foregoing. The prophet expostulates with God concerning the ways of Providence in permitting the wicked to prosper, <reference osisRef="Jer.12.1-Jer.12.4">Jer 12:1-4</reference>. It is intimated to him that he must endure still greater trials, <reference osisRef="Jer.12.5">Jer 12:5</reference>, from his false and deceitful brethren, <reference osisRef="Jer.12.6">Jer 12:6</reference>; but that still heavier judgments awaited the nation for their crimes, <reference osisRef="Jer.12.7-Jer.12.13">Jer 12:7-13</reference>. That God, however, would at length have compassion on them; restore them to their land; and turn his judgments against those that oppressed them, if not prevented by their becoming converts to the true religion, <reference osisRef="Jer.12.14-Jer.12.17">Jer 12:14-17</reference>. <div eID="gen29563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29564" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen29564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29565" type="x-p"/> Righteous art thou, O Lord, when I plead with thee - The prophet was grieved at the prosperity of the wicked; and he wonders how, consistently with God's righteousness, vice should often be in affluence, and piety in suffering and poverty. He knows that God is righteous, that every thing is done well; but he wishes to inquire how these apparently unequal and undeserved lots take place. On this subject he wishes to reason with God, that he may receive instruction.
entries.0c8f4de416f81f0ed235687a53cd70c469fa89c8: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen29565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29566" type="x-p"/> Thou art near in their mouth - They have no sincerity: they have something of the form of religion, but nothing of its power.
entries.cccc9b0e464acfdc2f3dc8a35133fd28b3bd108b: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen29566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29567" type="x-p"/> But thou, O Lord, knowest me - I know that the very secrets of my heart are known to thee; and I am glad of it, for thou knowest that my heart is towards thee - is upright and sincere.
entries.f0e418b83c7a2e569b39715e81bdb6666530d8d3: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen29567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29568" type="x-p"/> How long shall the land mourn - These hypocrites and open sinners are a curse to the country; pull them out, Lord, that the land may be delivered of that which is the cause of its desolation.
entries.b026d717bda3a68d4f441903926dce9e9becc99f: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen29568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29569" type="x-p"/> If thou hast run with the footmen - If the smallest evils to which thou art exposed cause thee to make so many bitter complaints, how wilt thou feel when, in the course of thy prophetic ministry, thou shalt be exposed to much greater, from enemies much more powerful? Footmen may here be the symbol of common evil events; horsemen, of evils much more terrible. If thou have sunk under small difficulties, what wilt thou do when great ones come? <div eID="gen29569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29570" type="x-p"/> And if in the land of peace, wherein thou trustedst - I believe the meaning is this, "If in a country now enjoying peace thou scarcely thinkest thyself in safety, what wilt thou do in the swellings of Jordan? in the time when the enemy, like an overflowing torrent, shall deluge every part of the land?" <div eID="gen29570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29571" type="x-p"/> The overflowing of Jordan, which generally happened in harvest, drove the lions and other beasts of prey from their coverts among the bushes that lined its banks; who, spreading themselves through the country, made terrible havoc, slaying men, and carrying off the cattle. <div eID="gen29571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29572" type="x-p"/> Perhaps by footmen may be meant the Philistines, Edomites, etc., whose armies were composed principally of infantry; and by the horses, the Chaldeans, who had abundance of cavalry and chariots in their army. But still the words are proverbial, and the above is their meaning.
entries.0411846237262e69768e4c5c370fbaadd63c70b8: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen29572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29573" type="x-p"/> For even thy brethren, and the house of thy father - Thou hast none to depend on but God: even thy brethren will betray thee when they have it in their power. <div eID="gen29573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29574" type="x-p"/> Believe them not - Do not trust to them, do not commit thyself to them; they are in heart thy enemies, and will betray thee.
entries.520a6120208c17a055b4b46d2b4554bf4d1a5ee6: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen29574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29575" type="x-p"/> I have forsaken mine house - I have abandoned my temple. <div eID="gen29575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29576" type="x-p"/> I have given the dearly beloved of my soul - The people once in covenant with me, and inexpressibly dear to me while faithful. <div eID="gen29576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29577" type="x-p"/> Into the hand of her enemies - This was a condition in the covenant I made with them; If they forsook me, they were to be abandoned to their enemies, and cast out of the good land I gave to their fathers.
entries.3c43e3dc3254755937e8f4678ee87f8e98e8b388: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen29577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29578" type="x-p"/> Mine heritage is unto me as a lion - The people are enraged against me; they roar like a furious lion against their God. They have proceeded to the most open acts of the most flagrant iniquity.
entries.7cee61375cc1badbc3454e5d80feb791cb5ce5c9: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen29578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29579" type="x-p"/> Is unto me as a speckled bird - A bird of divers colors. This is a people who have corrupted the worship of the true God with heathenish rites and ceremonies; therefore, the different nations, (see <reference osisRef="Jer.12.10">Jer 12:10</reference>; whose gods and forms of worship they have adopted shall come and spoil them. As far as you have followed the surrounding nations in their worship, so far shall they prevail over your state. Every one shall take that which is his own; and wherever he finds his own gods, he will consider the land consecrated to them, and take it as his property, because those very gods are the objects of his worship. The fable of the daw and borrowed plumes is no mean illustration of this passage. <div eID="gen29579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29580" type="x-p"/> Dahler translates the whole verse thus: - <div eID="gen29580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29581" type="x-p"/> Birds of prey! inundate with blood my heritage. <div eID="gen29581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29582" type="x-p"/> Birds of prey! come against her from all sides. <div eID="gen29582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29583" type="x-p"/> Run together in crowds, ye savage beasts! <div eID="gen29583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29584" type="x-p"/> Come to the carnage!
entries.6111d007730680bf99982722511f8a78a2a90d40: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen29584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29585" type="x-p"/> Many pastors have destroyed my vineyard - My people have had many kinds of enemies which have fed upon their richest pastures; the Philistines, the Moabites, Ammonites, Assyrians, Egyptians. and now the Chaldeans.
entries.f11e1572256b3ee4cdab0b6d001274d82f5cf0db: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen29585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29586" type="x-p"/> No man layeth it to heart - Notwithstanding all these desolations, from which the land every where mourns, and which are so plainly the consequences of the people's crimes, no man layeth it to heart, or considereth that these are God's judgments; and that the only way to have them removed is to repent of their sins, and turn to God with all their hearts.
entries.78488addf2b1a322ac7132824a35f3de8137fe07: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen29586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29587" type="x-p"/> The sword of the Lord shall devour - It is the sword of the Lord that has devoured, and will devour: this is what no man layeth to heart. They think these things come in the course of events.
entries.cfd1a57c11147add9af6b780e81b96762d7cd755: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen29587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29588" type="x-p"/> They have sown wheat, but shall reap thorns - All their projects shall fail: none of their enterprises shall succeed. They are enemies to God, and therefore cannot have his blessing.
entries.b95b230b91d01d1a505b485d33b7992eae9f68e1: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen29588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29589" type="x-p"/> Against all mine evil neighbors - All the neighboring nations who have united in desolating Judea shall be desolated in their turn: they also are wicked, and they shall be punished. If I make them executors of my justice, it is to them no proof of my approbation. God often uses one wicked nation to scourge another; and afterwards scourges the scourger by some other scourge. In some places a felon who was condemned to be hanged is made the common hangman for the county; he himself being still under the sentence of death, - <div eID="gen29589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29590" type="x-p"/> Till soon some trusty brother of the trade <div eID="gen29590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29591" type="x-p"/> Shall do for him what he has done for others.
entries.eb15cddd32fa670a053f79836e4e7e4833975f1e: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen29591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29592" type="x-p"/> I will return, and have compassion on them - This is a promise of restoration from the captivity, and an intimation also that some of their enemies would turn to the true God with them; learn the ways of his people; that is, would abjure idols, and take Jehovah for their God; and be built in the midst of his people, that is, Jew and Gentile forming one Church of the Most High.
entries.0e20f801266e2670fc2a14f9902100c8a8882014: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen29592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29593" type="x-p"/> I will - destroy that nation - Several of them did not obey, and are destroyed. Of the Moabites, Ammonites, and Chaldeans, not one vestige remains. The sixteenth verse is supposed to be a promise of the conversion of the Gentiles. See <reference osisRef="Eph.2.13-Eph.2.22">Eph 2:13-22</reference>. <div eID="gen29593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29594" type="x-p"/> From the thirteenth verse to the end is a different discourse, and Dahler supposes it to have been delivered in the seventh or eighth year of the reign of Jehoiakim.  <chapter eID="Jer.12"/> <div eID="gen29594" type="x-p"/>

entries.c003d109395097413346e21bb26b2495282c7c1a: <reference osisRef="Jer.12.1">Jer 12:1</reference> <hi type="italic">"Righteous art Thou, Jahveh, if I contend with Thee; yet will I plead with Thee in words. Wherefore doth the way of the wicked prosper, are all secure that deal faithlessly?</hi> Jer 12:2. <hi type="italic">Thou hast planted them, yea, they have taken root; grow, yea, bring forth fruit. Near art Thou in their mouth, yet far from their reins.</hi> Jer 12:3. <hi type="italic">But Thou, Jahveh, knowest me, seest me, and triest mine heart toward Thee. Tear them away like sheep to the slaughter, and devote them for a day of slaughter.</hi> Jer 12:4. <hi type="italic">How long is the earth to mourn and the herb of the field to wither? For the wickedness of them that dwell therein, gone are cattle and fowl; for they say: He sees not our end.</hi> Jer 12:5. <hi type="italic">If with the footmen thou didst run and they wearied thee, how couldst thou contend with the horses? and if thou trustest in the land of peace, how wilt thou do in the glory of Jordan?</hi> Jer 12:6. <hi type="italic">For even thy brethren and they father’s house, even they are faithless towards thee, yea, they call after thee with full voice. Believe them not, though they speak friendly to thee."</hi> <div eID="gen13968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13969" type="x-p"/> The prophet’s complaint begins by acknowledging: Thou art righteous, Lord, if I would dispute with Thee, i.e., would accuse Thee of injustice. I could convict Thee of no wrong; Thou wouldst appear righteous and prove Thyself in the right. <reference osisRef="Ps.51.6">Psa 51:6</reference>; Job 9:2. With אך comes in a limitation: only he will speak pleas of right, maintain a suit with Jahveh, will set before Him something that seems incompatible with God’s justice, namely the question: Why the way of the wicked prospers, why they that act faithlessly are in ease and comfort? On this cf. Job 21:7., where Job sets forth at length the contradiction between the prosperity of the wicked and the justice of God’s providence. The way of the wicked is the course of their life, their conduct. God has planted them, i.e., has placed them in their circumstances of life; like a tree they have struck root into the ground; they go on, i.e., grow, and bear fruit, i.e., their undertakings succeed, although they have God in their mouth only, not in their heart.
entries.fa360c26b8678687aaa52b58ae738507a63fa91f: <reference osisRef="Jer.12.3">Jer 12:3</reference> <div eID="gen13969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13970" type="x-p"/> To show that he has cause for his question, Jeremiah appeals to the omniscience of the Searcher of hearts. God knows him, tries his heart, and therefore knows how it is disposed towards Himself (אתּך belongs to לבּי, and את indicating the relation - here, viz., fidelity - in which the heart stands to God; cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.17">2Sa 16:17</reference>). Thus God knows that in his heart there is no unfaithfulness, and that he maintains to God an attitude altogether other than that of those hypocrites who have God on their lips only; and knows too the enmity which, without having provoked it, he experiences. How then comes it about that with the prophet it goes ill, while with those faithless ones it goes well? God, as the righteous God, must remove this contradiction. And so his request concludes: Tear them out (נתק of the tearing out of roots, <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.9">Eze 17:9</reference>); here Hiph. with the same force (pointing back to the metaphor of their being rooted, <reference osisRef="Jer.12.2">Jer 12:2</reference>), implying total destruction. Hence also the illustration: as sheep, that are dragged away out of the flock to be slaughtered. Devote them for the day of slaughter, like animals devoted to sacrifice.
entries.5a4cc812840ac98910f39d7c52743da981b41ad1: <reference osisRef="Jer.12.4">Jer 12:4</reference> <div eID="gen13970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13971" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Jer.12.4">Jer 12:4</reference> gives the motive of his prayer: How long shall the earth suffer from the wickedness of these hypocrites? be visited with drought and dearth for their sins? This question is not to be taken as a complaint that God is punishing without end; Hitz. so takes it, and then proposes to delete it as being out of all connection in sense with <reference osisRef="Jer.12.3">Jer 12:3</reference> or Jer 12:5. It is a complaint because of the continuance of God’s chastisement, drawn down by the wickedness of the apostates, which are bringing the land to utter ruin. The mourning of the land and the withering of the herb is a consequence of great drought; and the drought is a divine chastisement: cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.3.3">Jer 3:3</reference>; Jer 5:24., Jer 14:2., etc. But this falls not only on the unfaithful, but upon the godly too, and even the beasts, cattle, and birds suffer from it; and so the innocent along with the guilty. There seems to be injustice in this. To put an end to this injustice, to rescue the innocent from the curse brought by the wickedness of the ungodly, the prophet seeks the destruction of the wicked. ספה, to be swept away. The 3rd pers. fem. sing. with the plural ות-, as in <reference osisRef="Joel.1.20">Joe 1:20</reference> and often; cf. Ew. §317, <hi type="italic">a</hi>, Gesen. §146, 3. "They that dwell therein" are inhabitants of the land at large, the ungodly multitude of the people, of whom it is said in the last clause: they say, He will not see our end. The sense of these words is determined by the subject. Many follow the lxx (οὐκ ὄψεται ὁ Θεὸς ὁδοὺς ἡμῶν) and refer the seeing to God. God will not see their end, i.e., will not trouble Himself about it (Schnur., Ros., and others), or will not pay any heed to their future fate, so that they may do all they choose unpunished (Ew.). But to this Graf has justly objected, that ראה, in all the passages that can be cited for this sense of the word, is used only of that which God sees, regards as already present, never of that which is future. "He sees" is to be referred to the prophet. Of him the ungodly say, he shall not see their end, because they intend to put him out of the way (Hitz.); or better, in a less special sense, they ridicule the idea that his prophecies will be fulfilled, and say: He shall not see our end, because his threatenings will not come to pass.
entries.759cdcb43eadd14ccc28bedfb94d9f3dc8c73d23: <reference osisRef="Jer.12.5-Jer.12.6">Jer 12:5-6</reference> <div eID="gen13971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13972" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Jer.12.5">Jer 12:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.12.6">Jer 12:6</reference> the Lord so answers the prophet’s complaint as to reprove his impatience, by intimating that he will have to endure still worse. Both parts of <reference osisRef="Jer.12.5">Jer 12:5</reference> are of the nature of proverbs. If even the race with footmen made him weary, how will he be able to compete with horses? תּחרה here and <reference osisRef="Jer.22.15">Jer 22:15</reference>, a Tiph., Aramaic form for Hiph., arising by the hardening of the ה into ת-cf. Hos 11:3, and Ew. §122, <hi type="italic">a - </hi>rival, vie with. The proverb exhibits the contrast between tasks of smaller and greater difficulty, applied to the prophet’s relation to his enemies. What Jeremiah had to suffer from his countrymen at Anathoth was but a trifle compared with the malign assaults that yet awaited him in the discharge of his office. The second comparison conveys the same thought, but with a clearer intimation of the dangers the prophet will undergo. If thou puttest thy trust in a peaceful land, there alone countest on living in peace and safety, how wilt thou bear thyself in the glory of Jordan? The latter phrase does not mean the swelling of Jordan, its high flood, so as that we should with Umbr. and Ew., have here to think of the danger arising from a great and sudden inundation. It is the strip of land along the bank of the Jordan, thickly overgrown with shrubs, trees, and tall reeds, the lower valley, flooded when the river was swollen, where lions had their haunt, as in the reedy thickets of the Euphrates. Cf. v. Schubert, <hi type="italic">Resie</hi>, iii. S. 82; Robins. <hi type="italic">Bibl. Researches in Palestine</hi>, i. 535, and <hi type="italic">Phys. Geogr. of the Holy Land</hi>, p. 147. The "pride of the Jordan" is therefore mentioned in <reference osisRef="Jer.49.19">Jer 49:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.44">Jer 50:44</reference>; Zec 11:3, as the haunt of lions, and comes before us here as a region where men’s lives were in danger. The point of the comparison is accordingly this: Thy case up till this time is, in spite of the onsets thou hast borne, to be compared to a sojourn in a peaceful land; but thou shalt come into much sorer case, where thou shalt never for a moment be sure of thy life. To illustrate this, he is told in <reference osisRef="Jer.12.6">Jer 12:6</reference> that his nearest of kin, and those dwelling under the same roof, will behave unfaithfully towards him. They will cry behind him מלא, <hi type="italic">plena voce</hi> (Jerome; cf. קראוּ מלאוּ, <reference osisRef="Jer.4.5">Jer 4:5</reference>). They will cry after him, "as one cries when pursuing a thief or murderer" (Gr.). Perfectly apposite is therefore Luther’s translation: They set up a hue and cry after thee. These words are not meant to be literally taken, but convey the thought, that even his nearest friends will persecute him as a malefactor. It is therefore a perverse design that seeks to find the distinction between the inhabitants of Anathoth and the brethren and housemates, in a contrast between the priests and the blood-relations. Although Anathoth was a city of the priests, the men of Anathoth need not have been all priests, since these cities were not exclusively occupied by priests. - In this reproof of the prophet there lies not merely the truth that much sorer suffering yet awaits him, but the truth besides, that the people’s faithlessness and wickedness towards God and men will yet grow greater, ere the judgment of destruction fall upon Judah; for the divine long-suffering is not yet exhausted, nor has ungodliness yet fairly reached its highest point, so that the final destruction must straightway be carried out. But judgment will not tarry long.
